name: Pentecost: the Church begins
date_text: c. AD 30–33 (the year is not known)
summary: Fifty days after the Resurrection the Holy Spirit comes on the apostles in Jerusalem; Peter preaches and about three thousand are baptised (Acts 2). The Church keeps this as its birthday.

name: The Council of Jerusalem
summary: The apostles and elders meet over whether Gentile converts must keep the Law of Moses; they decide not to lay that burden on them. The pattern of a council deciding together begins here.

name: Nero's persecution; Peter and Paul martyred in Rome
date_basis: documented (Tacitus); the apostles' deaths by tradition
summary: After the great fire of Rome Nero blames the Christians, who are killed in large numbers. By tradition Peter is crucified and Paul beheaded in Rome in these years.

name: The Temple in Jerusalem destroyed
summary: Roman forces under Titus take Jerusalem and burn the Temple; Christianity and Judaism go on their separate ways.

name: First Clement: Rome writes to Corinth
summary: The church at Rome, through Clement, writes to Corinth after the presbyters there were deposed; one of the earliest Christian writings outside the New Testament.

name: Martyrdom of Ignatius of Antioch
summary: The bishop of Antioch is taken to Rome to die in the arena, writing seven letters on the way: the first to speak of "the catholic Church" and of one bishop in each church.

name: Martyrdom of Polycarp of Smyrna
date_basis: documented (The Martyrdom of Polycarp); year disputed
summary: The aged bishop of Smyrna, a disciple of the apostle John, is burned for refusing to curse Christ: "Eighty-six years I have served him." The earliest account of a martyrdom kept by a church.

name: The persecution of Decius
summary: Every citizen must sacrifice to the gods and carry a certificate saying so. Many Christians lapse; quarrels over receiving them back split the Church at Rome and Carthage.

name: Cyprian writes On the Unity of the Church
summary: In the schisms after Decius, the bishop of Carthage writes that there is one Church as there is one Christ: "He cannot have God for his Father who has not the Church for his mother." Read it on the Writings shelf.

name: Martyrdom of Cyprian
summary: Under Valerian, Cyprian is beheaded outside Carthage: the first bishop of Africa to die a martyr.

name: Antony goes into the desert
summary: Hearing "go, sell what you have", the young Egyptian Antony gives away his land and goes into the desert; others follow, and monasticism begins. His life is on the Writings shelf.

name: Armenia becomes a Christian kingdom
summary: King Tiridates III is baptised by Gregory the Illuminator; Armenia is counted the first state to take Christianity as its own.

name: The Great Persecution under Diocletian
summary: The last and fiercest persecution: churches destroyed, scriptures burned, clergy imprisoned and many martyrs, until Galerius' edict of toleration in 311.

name: The Edict of Milan
summary: Constantine and Licinius agree to tolerate all religions and return Christian property. The age of the martyrs ends.

name: The First Ecumenical Council, Nicaea
summary: Called by Constantine against the teaching of Arius that the Son was created. The council confesses the Son "of one essence (homoousios) with the Father", writes the first form of the Creed and settles the date of Pascha. Its canons are on the Writings shelf.

name: Constantinople founded as the new capital
summary: Constantine dedicates the city on the site of Byzantium: the "New Rome" and for over a thousand years the centre of the Orthodox world.

name: Georgia turns to Christ
summary: Through the preaching of St Nino, King Mirian III of Iberia is baptised and Christianity becomes the faith of the Georgian kingdom.

name: Antony dies; Athanasius writes his Life
summary: Antony dies aged about 105. Athanasius' Life of Antony, soon read across East and West, makes the desert life known everywhere.

name: Athanasius lists the 27 books of the New Testament
summary: In his 39th Festal Letter Athanasius names the 27 books now in every New Testament, the first list to match it exactly.

name: Basil writes On the Holy Spirit
summary: Basil defends glorifying the Holy Spirit together with the Father and the Son. With the two Gregorys (the Cappadocians) he gives the Church the language of one essence and three persons (hypostases). On the Writings shelf.

name: The Second Ecumenical Council, Constantinople I
summary: Theodosius I calls the bishops of the East. Gregory the Theologian presides for a time; the council confirms Nicaea and completes the Creed on the Holy Spirit, "the Lord, the Giver of Life". The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed is the one said at every Liturgy.

name: Chrysostom preaches the Homilies on the Statues
summary: Antioch riots over a new tax and throws down the emperor's statues; through Lent, while the city waits for punishment, the priest John preaches twenty-one sermons. On the Writings shelf.

name: John Chrysostom, archbishop of Constantinople
summary: The preacher of Antioch is made archbishop of the capital; his calls to reform and his rebukes of the court lead to two exiles. He dies on the road, saying "Glory to God for all things."

name: The Third Ecumenical Council, Ephesus
summary: Against Nestorius, the council led by Cyril of Alexandria confesses one Christ, the Word made flesh, and the Virgin Mary as Theotokos, the one who gave birth to God. The Church of the East does not accept it.

name: The Fourth Ecumenical Council, Chalcedon
summary: The council confesses one Christ "in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation"; canon 28 gives Constantinople rank after Rome. The Coptic, Syriac, Armenian and Ethiopian churches do not receive it (the Oriental Orthodox). Orthodox view: the faith of the fathers rightly defined; dialogues since the 1960s have found much of the dispute to be over words.

name: The last Western emperor deposed
summary: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus. The empire goes on in the East, centred on Constantinople; what the West later calls the Byzantine Empire called itself Roman.

name: Hagia Sophia dedicated
summary: Justinian dedicates the Great Church of Holy Wisdom, for nine centuries the largest church in the world and the cathedral of the Ecumenical Patriarch.

name: The Fifth Ecumenical Council, Constantinople II
summary: Justinian's council condemns the "Three Chapters" (writings held to favour Nestorius) and, with it, teachings of Origen. Its anathemas are on the Writings shelf; it made no disciplinary canons.

name: The Sixth Ecumenical Council, Constantinople III
summary: Christ has two wills and two energies, divine and human, the human freely following the divine: the faith Maximus the Confessor died for. The council condemns monothelitism and Pope Honorius.

name: The Council in Trullo (Quinisext)
summary: A council in the domed hall (trullus) of the palace makes the 102 canons the Orthodox Church counts as those of the fifth and sixth councils. Rome never fully received them. On the Writings shelf.

name: Iconoclasm begins
summary: Emperor Leo III acts against the holy icons; in 730 an edict forbids them. John of Damascus, under Muslim rule and out of the emperor's reach, writes his three treatises defending them.

name: John of Damascus writes the Exact Exposition
summary: The monk of Mar Saba gathers the teaching of the fathers into one hundred chapters, the first summary of Orthodox doctrine. On the Writings shelf.

name: The Seventh Ecumenical Council, Nicaea II
summary: Called by the Empress Irene: the holy icons are to be venerated, the honour passing to the one shown, while worship is for God alone. The last council the Orthodox Church counts as ecumenical.

name: Charlemagne crowned emperor in Rome
summary: Pope Leo III crowns the Frankish king emperor, a rival to the emperor in Constantinople. The Frankish church's addition of the Filioque ("and the Son") to the Creed becomes a lasting dispute.

name: The Triumph of Orthodoxy
summary: The Empress Theodora and Patriarch Methodios restore the icons for good. The Orthodox Church keeps the first Sunday of Great Lent as the Sunday of Orthodoxy.

name: Photius patriarch: the first quarrel with Rome
summary: Photius is made patriarch in place of Ignatius; Pope Nicholas I refuses to recognise him. In 867 Photius condemns the Filioque and Frankish missions in Bulgaria. Orthodox view: Photius, a saint, defended the Creed as the councils left it; Rome long counted him a schismatic.

name: Cyril and Methodius go to the Slavs
summary: Sent by Photius at Prince Rastislav's request, the brothers of Thessalonica bring the Gospel and the Liturgy in the Slavs' own tongue, with an alphabet made for it.

name: Bulgaria baptised
summary: Khan Boris I is baptised from Constantinople; the disciples of Cyril and Methodius later make Bulgaria the centre of Slavonic Christian letters.

name: The Great Lavra founded on Mount Athos
summary: Athanasius the Athonite founds the first great monastery of the Holy Mountain, which becomes the heart of Orthodox monasticism.

name: The Baptism of Rus'
summary: Grand Prince Vladimir of Kiev is baptised and the people of Kiev in the Dnieper after him. Rus' takes its faith from Constantinople: the origin of the Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian churches.

name: Symeon the New Theologian dies
summary: The abbot of St Mamas taught that the vision of God's uncreated light is for every Christian, not the saints of old only; a forerunner of the hesychasts.

name: The Great Schism
summary: Cardinal Humbert lays a bull excommunicating Patriarch Michael Cerularius on the altar of Hagia Sophia; the patriarch's synod answers with its own. The quarrel (the Pope's claims, the Filioque, unleavened bread) hardens over the next centuries into the division of East and West. Orthodox view: Rome departed from the faith and order of the councils; the Catholic Church sees it otherwise.

name: The First Crusade takes Jerusalem
summary: Answering the Byzantine call for help against the Seljuks, Western armies take Antioch and Jerusalem and set up Latin patriarchs in place of Greek ones.

name: The Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
summary: Crusaders bound for Egypt turn on Constantinople and plunder it for three days; a Latin emperor and patriarch rule until 1261. Orthodox view: the moment the schism entered the hearts of the people. In 2001 and 2004 Pope John Paul II expressed sorrow for it.

name: The Serbian Church becomes autocephalous
summary: St Sava is consecrated first archbishop of an autocephalous (self-governing) Serbian Church by the patriarch in exile at Nicaea.

name: Constantinople recovered from the Latins
summary: Michael VIII Palaiologos's forces retake the city; the Orthodox patriarch returns.

name: The hesychast councils uphold Gregory Palamas
summary: Against Barlaam, Palamas defends the monks of Athos who pray the Jesus Prayer in stillness (hesychia): God is unknowable in his essence but truly known in his uncreated energies, the light of Tabor. Councils in Constantinople uphold him.

name: The Council of Florence
summary: In need of Western help against the Turks, the Byzantine emperor and bishops sign a union with Rome; Mark of Ephesus alone refuses. At home clergy and people reject it. Orthodox view: a false union, rightly refused; the Catholic Church counts Florence an ecumenical council.

name: The Church of Moscow chooses its own metropolitan
summary: After the union of Florence, Russian bishops elect Jonah metropolitan without Constantinople: the start of the Russian Church's independence.

name: The Fall of Constantinople
summary: Mehmed II takes the city; the last emperor, Constantine XI, dies on the walls. Hagia Sophia becomes a mosque.

name: Gennadios Scholarios, patriarch under the Sultan
summary: Mehmed II has the opponent of Florence made patriarch and head of all Orthodox Christians in the empire (the Rum millet): the Church is to carry its people through four centuries of Ottoman rule.

name: Luther posts the Ninety-five Theses
summary: Martin Luther challenges the sale of indulgences; the Protestant Reformation begins and the Western Church divides again.

name: Calvin's Institutes
summary: The Reformed tradition's great work of doctrine, enlarged through five editions. Beveridge's translation is on the Writings shelf.

name: The Council of Trent
summary: The Catholic Church answers the Reformation, defining its teaching on scripture and tradition, justification and the sacraments.

name: The Moscow Patriarchate
summary: Patriarch Jeremias II of Constantinople raises Job, metropolitan of Moscow, to patriarch; councils of the Eastern patriarchs confirm it in 1590 and 1593.

name: The Union of Brest
summary: Most Orthodox bishops of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth enter communion with Rome, keeping their Byzantine rite: the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church. Orthodox view: a union imposed from above that many clergy and faithful refused.

name: Nikon's reforms and the Old Believers
summary: Patriarch Nikon brings Russian service books and customs into line with the Greek; those who refuse, the Old Believers, are condemned at the councils of 1666–1667.

name: Peter the Great abolishes the patriarchate
summary: The Russian Church is governed by a Holy Synod under a lay official of the state until 1917.

name: The Philokalia published
summary: Nikodemos the Hagiorite and Macarius of Corinth publish in Venice the Philokalia, texts of the fathers on watchfulness and prayer from the 4th to the 15th centuries; Paisius Velichkovsky's Slavonic version follows in 1793.

name: Missionaries reach Alaska
summary: Monks of Valaam, among them St Herman, arrive on Kodiak: the start of Orthodoxy in North America.

name: The Pedalion (the Rudder) published
summary: Nikodemos' edition of the canons of the apostles, councils and fathers with commentary: the handbook of canon law of the Greek-speaking churches.

name: The Church of Greece declares autocephaly
summary: After independence from the Ottomans the Greek kingdom's church declares itself self-governing; the Ecumenical Patriarchate recognises it by tomos in 1850.

name: The Bulgarian Exarchate
summary: The Sultan allows a Bulgarian church separate from the patriarch; Constantinople declares it schismatic in 1872, a breach healed in 1945. The Bulgarian Patriarchate is restored in 1953.

name: Serbia's church recognised as autocephalous
summary: After Serbian independence the Ecumenical Patriarchate recognises the Metropolitanate of Belgrade as autocephalous; the Serbian Patriarchate is restored in 1920.

name: The Romanian Church recognised as autocephalous
summary: Constantinople grants the tomos of autocephaly; the Romanian Patriarchate follows in 1925.

name: Hapgood's Service Book
summary: Isabel Hapgood publishes the first English book of Orthodox services, with the blessing of Archbishop (later Patriarch) Tikhon. On the Writings shelf.

name: The patriarchate restored; Tikhon elected
summary: The All-Russian Council restores the patriarchate, and Tikhon is chosen by lot days after the Bolshevik revolution.

name: The Soviet persecution
summary: Church and state are separated and church property seized; in the 1920s and 1930s tens of thousands of clergy, monks and lay people are shot or die in the camps, and nearly every church is closed. The Russian Church has since glorified over a thousand of them as New Martyrs and Confessors.

name: The Russian Church Abroad organised
summary: Bishops who fled the revolution meet in Serbia and form what becomes the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia; the emigration plants Orthodox parishes across Europe and the Americas.

name: The Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America
summary: Constantinople founds an archdiocese for the Greek immigrants of North and South America.

name: St Silouan the Athonite dies
summary: The Russian monk of St Panteleimon dies; his disciple Sophrony publishes his life and teaching, and Constantinople glorifies him as a saint in 1987. (His writings are modern and copyrighted, so they are not on the shelf.)

name: Munich Agreement
summary: Britain, France and Italy agree that Germany may take the Sudetenland; Czechoslovakia is not asked. Chamberlain calls it "peace for our time".

name: Nazi–Soviet Pact
summary: Germany and the USSR promise not to fight each other; a secret protocol divides Poland and the Baltic states between them.

name: Germany invades Poland
summary: German forces cross into Poland; the USSR invades from the east on 17 September.

name: Britain and France declare war on Germany
summary: Germany ignores the demand to leave Poland, and Britain and France declare war.

name: Battle of the Atlantic
summary: The longest campaign of the war: U-boats against the convoys carrying food, fuel and arms to Britain.

name: Dunkirk evacuation
summary: Operation Dynamo: about 338,000 British and French troops are taken off the beaches by warships and small boats.

name: Fall of France
summary: After six weeks of fighting France signs an armistice; Germany occupies the north and west.

name: Battle of Britain
summary: The RAF defeats the Luftwaffe's attempt to win control of the air, so the invasion of Britain is put off.

name: The Blitz
summary: German bombing of British cities, by night; about 43,000 civilians are killed.

name: Lend-Lease Act
summary: The USA agrees to lend or lease war supplies to Britain and, later, the USSR and others, without payment up front.

name: Operation Barbarossa
summary: Germany invades the USSR, breaking the pact of 1939; the attack is stopped short of Moscow in December.

name: Attack on Pearl Harbor
summary: Japanese aircraft attack the US fleet; the next day the USA declares war on Japan, and on 11 December Germany declares war on the USA.

name: Wannsee Conference
summary: Nazi officials coordinate the "Final Solution", the plan to murder the Jews of Europe.

name: Battle of Midway
summary: US carrier aircraft sink four Japanese carriers; Japan's advance in the Pacific is checked.

name: Battle of Stalingrad
summary: The Red Army surrounds the German Sixth Army in the city, which surrenders: the turning point in the east.

name: Second Battle of El Alamein
summary: The Eighth Army breaks Rommel's line in Egypt and the Axis retreat across North Africa begins.

name: Battle of Kursk
summary: The last great German offensive in the east fails; the largest tank battle of the war.

name: Italian armistice
summary: Italy surrenders to the Allies, five weeks after Mussolini is removed; German troops occupy the north.

name: Stalin allows a patriarch again
summary: In the war Stalin lets a council meet; Sergius is elected patriarch, and some churches and seminaries reopen under state control.

name: D-Day
summary: Operation Overlord begins: Allied troops land on five Normandy beaches, opening the second front in the west.

name: Yalta Conference
summary: Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin plan the end of the war: Germany to be divided, free elections promised in eastern Europe.

name: Death of Hitler
summary: With the Red Army fighting in Berlin, Hitler kills himself in his bunker.

name: VE Day
summary: Germany's unconditional surrender, signed at Reims on 7 May, takes effect: Victory in Europe.

name: Potsdam Conference
summary: Truman, Stalin and Churchill (then Attlee) settle the occupation of Germany and call on Japan to surrender.

name: Atomic bombing of Hiroshima
summary: A US bomber drops the first atomic bomb used in war on Hiroshima.

name: Atomic bombing of Nagasaki
summary: A second atomic bomb is dropped, on Nagasaki; the USSR had declared war on Japan the day before.

name: Japan surrenders (VJ Day)
summary: Emperor Hirohito announces Japan's surrender; it is signed aboard USS Missouri on 2 September, ending the war.

name: Sophrony founds the monastery in Essex
summary: Archimandrite Sophrony, disciple of St Silouan, founds the Patriarchal Stavropegic Monastery of St John the Baptist in England.

name: Athenagoras and Paul VI meet in Jerusalem
summary: The first meeting of a pope and an ecumenical patriarch since 1439.

name: The anathemas of 1054 lifted
summary: A joint declaration of Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras removes the excommunications of 1054 "from the memory of the Church". Orthodox view: a gesture of charity; communion still waits on agreement in faith.

name: The Orthodox Church in America made autocephalous by Moscow
summary: Moscow grants autocephaly to its former North American metropolia; Constantinople and several other churches have not recognised it.

name: The millennium of the Baptism of Rus'
summary: The Soviet state allows the thousand-year celebration; churches reopen and the long revival of the Russian Church begins.

name: Bartholomew becomes Ecumenical Patriarch
summary: Bartholomew is elected the 270th archbishop of Constantinople.

name: Moscow and the Church Abroad reunited
summary: The Act of Canonical Communion ends some eighty years of separation.

name: The Holy and Great Council, Crete
summary: Ten of the fourteen autocephalous churches meet after decades of preparation; the churches of Antioch, Bulgaria, Georgia and Russia stay away, and do not receive it as binding.

name: Autocephaly for the Orthodox Church of Ukraine
summary: Constantinople decides to grant autocephaly in Ukraine; Moscow breaks communion with it (15 October 2018). A unification council founds the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (15 December) and receives the tomos. Views differ: Constantinople holds it the mother church's right; Moscow holds Ukraine its own territory. Some churches recognise the new church, others do not.

name: The Ukrainian Orthodox Church's council after the invasion
summary: After Russia's full-scale invasion, the council of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church long under Moscow declares its "full independence", without asking for autocephaly.

name: 1700 years since Nicaea
summary: Pope Leo XIV and Patriarch Bartholomew pray together at İznik, the old Nicaea, on the anniversary of the first council and say the Creed together.
